pageData.title: The Caral-Supe / Norte Chico Civilization
pageData.titleline: The Caral-Supe / Norte Chico Civilization - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Caral-Supe / Norte Chico Civilization. The Caral-Supe civilization - also known as the Norte Chico civilization - was a complex pre-Columbian society located in the Norte Chico region of what is now Peru, positioned to take advantage of three rivers: the Fortaleza, the Pativilca, and the Supe. Flourishing some 5,000 years ago, in the Late Archaic period of the central Andes, it has been established as the oldest known civilization in the Americas. This civilization matters because it proved that monumental urban architecture and complex social organization arose in the Americas extraordinarily early - and, unusually, without ceramics at its foundation, a society built instead on what its rivers, fields, and the nearby Pacific could provide.
pageData.para2: The city of Caral sits on a dry desert terrace overlooking the green valley of the Supe river, and features complex and monumental architecture, including six large pyramidal structures; the city's plan, its pyramids, and the elite residential group show clear evidence of ceremonial functions. Among the artifacts found at Caral is a quipu - a knotted textile piece that archaeologists believe was a method of keeping records - and a geoglyph was discovered just west of the city in 2000. Sophisticated government is assumed to have been required to manage the ancient Norte Chico, though questions remain over its organization, and notably, no evidence of warfare has been found. Its monumental scale and careful ceremonial planning continue to reveal the complexity of Caral society to archaeologists. Remarkably intact thanks to its early abandonment and late discovery, Caral was occupied only twice more, and never systematically, leaving its plazas and pyramids to sleep beneath the desert until modern archaeology woke them.
pageData.source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Sacred City of Caral-Supe (UNESCO/NHK)

pageData.title: The Chavín Culture
pageData.titleline: The Chavín Culture - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Chavin Culture. The Chavin culture was a highly developed civilization of pre-Columbian Peru that flourished between about 900 and 200 BCE, its artistic influence spreading throughout the northern and central Andes. Its great religious center, Chavin de Huantar, became an important Andean pilgrimage site - though the site may not have been the actual center of origin of the culture and its style, whose roots lie in the Initial Period (about 1800-900 BCE), when a sedentary agricultural way of life became fully established; important regional manifestations of the style are found at sites such as Kotosh. The significance of Chavin is that for the first time, many of the local and regional cultures of the area were unified by a common ideology or religion - a shared spiritual horizon whose imagery, from the Paracas to the Incas, helped spread Chavin ideas across the Andes and into later empires.
pageData.para2: At the heart of the religion stood the Staff Deity, associated with agricultural fertility and usually shown holding a staff in each hand - a forerunner of the Andean creator god Viracocha - celebrated in works like the Raimondi Stela, a two-metre granite slab with the god incised in low relief, and in carvings that form a transformational series changing progressively from human to jaguar form. The temple at Chavin de Huantar, measuring a hundred metres in length, enclosed its rites in complex interiors: an important feature of the cult was a priesthood of shamans who put themselves into trances with hallucinogens. Votive offerings from distant lowland jungles confirm the far-reaching influence of the cult. The site and the culture entered into decline sometime in the 3rd century BCE, for reasons that remain unknown.

pageData.title: The Moche Culture
pageData.titleline: The Moche Culture - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Moche Culture. The Moche culture was a sophisticated coastal civilization that flourished along the river valleys of northern Peru from the 1st to the 8th century CE, its influence reaching from the Piura valley south over 350 kilometers to the Nepena valley. They were intensive farmers, channeling streams from the Andes into irrigation canals to grow crops such as corn and beans, and with that agricultural wealth they supported urban centers and built impressive structures - adobe pyramids like the great Huaca del Sol and Huaca de la Luna, terraced platforms, palaces, courtyards, and plazas. This civilization matters because its artists produced what stands as some of the finest naturalistic pottery in pre-Columbian America - mold-made vessels with their characteristic stirrup spouts, portrait heads of people, animals, and plants, and painted scenes that open a window onto Moche ceremonial and daily life.
pageData.para2: Those painted vessels show a society that was aggressive and hierarchical: scenes of the sacrifice of prisoners and ritual combat, dignitaries in splendid regalia, and fortified structures - the Moche dispersed their communities to preserve precious irrigated land. Their burial traditions matched that hierarchy: at Huaca Rajada near Sipan, archaeologists uncovered elaborate tombs filled with jewelry, their occupants' skeletal remains suggesting men significantly taller than the average Moche adult, each tomb with a compartment containing miniature representations of the dead lord's world. Gold and copper alloy masks, regalia, and masterful metalwork accompanied them. The Moche world was eventually undone in part by the very forces that sustained it - the fragile ecology of desert valleys fed by Andean streams - leaving their adobe cities and painted lords to tell the tale of their world.

pageData.title: The Nazca Culture
pageData.titleline: The Nazca Culture - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Nazca Culture. The Nazca culture was an ancient civilization that flourished on the southern coast of Peru between 200 BCE and 600 CE, settling the Nazca valley and its neighbors - the Pisco, Chincha, Ica, Palpa, and Acari valleys - with their principal religious and urban sites at Cahuachi and Ventilla. Cahuachi, on the south bank of the Nazca River fifty kilometers inland, was a site of pilgrimage and the Nazca religious capital, where postholes suggest canopies once protected worshippers from the sun and textile scenes link religious gatherings to harvest festivals. The culture matters above all for the Nazca Lines: great geoglyphs etched into the desert floor - geometric shapes, or animals such as the hummingbird, the spider, even a killer whale - including straight lines up to twenty kilometers long whose exact purpose remains debated, perhaps connecting sacred sites or pointing to water sources.
pageData.para2: To survive under the present threat of drought, the Nazca built an extensive network of underground aqueducts, galleries, and cisterns to ensure a good water supply during the dry months. Their pottery is polychrome, sometimes modeled in the culture's later phases, and counted amongst the finest of ancient Peru, decorated with mythical transformational creatures - especially felines - and with trophy-heads, which also appear as miniature border decorations in their textiles; the presence of highland vicuna wool in those textiles is evidence of established trade with the highland cultures. Fine pottery and textiles were buried with the dead, with no particular distinction between male and female graves. In their ceramics, their featherwork, and their vast desert drawings, the Nazca left one of the most distinctive artistic legacies of the ancient Andes.

pageData.title: The Tiwanaku & Wari Empires
pageData.titleline: The Tiwanaku & Wari Empires - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Tiwanaku & Wari Empires. The Tiwanaku and Wari empires were the two great powers of the Andean Middle Horizon (600-1000 CE). Tiwanaku took its name from the ruins near the southern shore of Lake Titicaca in Bolivia - now a UNESCO World Heritage site - where its Kalasasaya platform and the structure known as the Palacio stand, the Kalasasaya holding the monolithic Gateway of the Sun, carved with a staff-carrying Doorway God flanked by winged figures, a god variously described as a Sun god or a thunder god. Wari, exploiting the diverse landscapes of Peru's coast and highlands as it flourished between about 450 and 1000 CE from its capital at Huari in the Peruvian highlands, constructed an empire administered by provincial capitals connected by a large road network - methods of maintaining an empire, and an artistic style, that would have a lasting influence on the Andes.
pageData.para2: Both states were gifted agriculturalists. The Wari constructed canals to irrigate terraced fields, and the economic stability this brought allowed them to resist the thirty-year drought at the end of the 6th century CE that contributed to the decline of their neighbors; at their administrative site of Pikillacta, with its strictly controlled single winding entrance, archaeologists found forty miniature greenstone figures of elite citizens. Their art centered on the Staff Deity, with plants, the San Pedro cactus flower, pumas, condors, and above all llamas - testimony to the importance of the herds. Why these empires fell is still debated: theories range from over-extension to another extended drought in the 9th century, but whatever the reasons, the region returned to a world of competing local powers until the rise of the Inca.
pageData.source4label: The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Central and Southern Andes, 500–1000 A.D.

pageData.title: The Valdivia Culture
pageData.titleline: The Valdivia Culture - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Valdivia culture of coastal Ecuador produced some of the oldest pottery in the Americas and one of the earliest village societies on the Pacific coast of South America. Flourishing from about 4400 to 1450 BCE along the fertile valleys of what are now Guayas and Manabí provinces, Valdivia communities lived in permanent villages of houses arranged around a central plaza, a layout that suggests organized social life long before cities appeared in the Andes. The largest known site, Real Alto, grew into a substantial ceremonial center with mound structures, housing perhaps a thousand or more people at its height.
pageData.para2: Valdivia people were skilled farmers and fishermen. They cultivated maize, beans, squash, and cotton in the river valleys and harvested the rich Pacific waters for fish and shellfish, leaving behind huge shell middens that archaeologists still study. Cotton was especially important, woven into textiles and fishing nets. This mixed economy of farming and fishing supported a settled, growing population centuries before comparable developments elsewhere in the region, and it made the Ecuadorian coast one of the earliest centers of sedentary life in the Americas.
pageData.para3: The culture is most famous for its ceramics. Valdivia potters produced elegant bowls and jars decorated with incised geometric designs, and they created thousands of small ceramic figurines, mostly female, often elaborately styled with detailed hairdos. These so-called Venus figurines are among the most celebrated artworks of ancient South America, though their purpose remains debated: they may have been used in fertility rites, healing ceremonies, or household rituals. Some were deliberately broken, perhaps as part of the ceremonies in which they were used.
pageData.para4: Valdivia pottery was once thought to show influence from the Jōmon culture of Japan, a theory that has since been discarded in favor of local development. As the culture declined after about 1450 BCE, its traditions fed into the succeeding Machalilla and Chorrera cultures of the Ecuadorian coast, and its ceramic and village-building legacy spread into the wider Andean world. The Valdivia culture demonstrated that complex, settled life on the Pacific coast of South America arose independently and remarkably early, thousands of years before the Inca.

pageData.title: The Paracas Culture
pageData.titleline: The Paracas Culture - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Paracas culture of Peru's south coast produced what many consider the finest textiles of the ancient Americas, woven masterpieces that preserved their brilliant colors for two thousand years in the dry desert soil. Occupying the Paracas Peninsula and the neighboring valleys from about 800 to 100 BCE, the Paracas people lived in one of the driest environments on Earth, where rain almost never falls. That extreme aridity, which made life hard, proved a gift to archaeologists, preserving textiles, mummies, and organic objects that would have rotted anywhere else.
pageData.para2: Paracas society is known mainly from its burials. The dead were wrapped in many layers of finely embroidered mantles, shirts, and headbands, then seated in baskets and placed in underground chambers. In 1925 the Peruvian archaeologist Julio C. Tello excavated the famous necropolis of Wari Kayan on the peninsula, finding 429 funerary bundles. Some elite individuals were wrapped in dozens of garments, forming conical mummy bundles. The embroidery depicts dazzling repeated figures: flying shamans, bird-men, felines, and supernatural beings with streaming appendages, worked in vividly dyed camelid fibers.
pageData.para3: Textiles were clearly central to Paracas life and belief, and their production involved huge communal labor: a single mantle could contain years of work. Scholars believe the embroidered images encoded religious ideas and myths that we can no longer read directly, since the Paracas left no writing. The culture also practiced cranial deformation, binding infants' heads to produce elongated skulls, and trephination, the surgical removal of sections of the skull, which many patients survived, as healed bone edges show.
pageData.para4: The Paracas peninsula's importance continued after the culture faded. Around 100 BCE the region gave way to the related Topará and then the Nazca culture, which inherited Paracas textile and ceramic traditions and later etched the famous Nazca Lines nearby. Julio Tello, Peru's first great Indigenous archaeologist, made the Paracas discoveries a cornerstone of Peruvian national identity, arguing that Andean civilization had deep coastal roots independent of outside influence. Many of the finest Paracas textiles are preserved today in museums in Lima and in collections around the world.

pageData.title: The Recuay and Cajamarca Cultures
pageData.titleline: The Recuay and Cajamarca Cultures - The History Web
pageData.para1: In the highlands of northern Peru, between the fall of the great Chavín cult and the rise of the Wari empire, two distinctive cultures flourished in the mountain basins: Recuay in the Callejón de Huaylas of Ancash, and Cajamarca in the fertile valley further north. Both developed during the Early Intermediate Period, roughly 200 BCE to 800 CE, when no single power ruled the Andes and regional styles blossomed in art and architecture. Though they never built empires, these highland societies produced remarkable stone buildings and ceramics and laid foundations later absorbed into larger states.
pageData.para2: The Recuay people lived in small hilltop settlements in the shadow of the Cordillera Blanca, Peru's highest mountain range. Their architecture featured multi-roomed stone structures with high-pitched roofs, and they built underground galleries and raised stone tombs for their dead. Recuay potters created a striking ceramic style, using fine white kaolin clay for vessels painted in black and red, often shaped as warriors, llamas, and architectural models of houses. These lively, sculptural pots give us snapshots of Recuay life: chieftains on stools, musicians, and loaded llamas like the caravans that still cross the highlands today.
pageData.para3: The Cajamarca culture developed in the valley of Cajamarca, which would centuries later become famous as the site of the Inca emperor Atahualpa's capture. Cajamarca potters perfected a brilliant cursive style, painting vessels with running, calligraphic designs of birds, flowers, and abstract motifs in black and orange on cream backgrounds. Their ceramics were so admired that they were traded widely across northern Peru and imitated by neighboring peoples. Cajamarca society was organized in small chiefdoms scattered across the valley, living from maize agriculture and llama herding in the high pastures.
pageData.para4: Both cultures eventually came under the influence of the Wari empire around 700-800 CE, which spread its own styles and administration through the highlands. Their traditions did not vanish but merged into the evolving highland world that would later produce kingdoms the Inca absorbed. The Recuay heartland today draws visitors to the same snowcapped Cordillera Blanca, while Cajamarca remains a prosperous agricultural city. Museums in Lima and Huaraz hold outstanding collections of Recuay warrior vessels and Cajamarca painted bowls.

pageData.title: The Chinchorro Culture
pageData.titleline: The Chinchorro Culture - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Chinchorro Culture. On the desert coast of what is now northern Chile and southern Peru, around seven thousand years ago, a people of fishers and hunters did something no one else on earth had yet thought to do: they deliberately preserved their dead. The Chinchorro mummies of Arica and Camarones are the oldest known artificial mummies in the world, older than Egypt's by some two thousand years, and the practice endured for nearly four thousand years, from about 5000 to 1500 BC.
pageData.para2: Chinchorro mummification was an astonishing craft. The earliest technique, the black mummies, involved disarticulating the body, removing the soft tissue, reinforcing the skeleton with sticks, and rebuilding the figure with clay and reeds before coating it in black manganese paste; later red mummies were painted over with ochre, their faces masked, their hair made of human wigs. Most striking of all, the Chinchorro did not reserve the rite for kings or priests: they mummified men, women, the elderly - and, with particular care, children and even miscarried infants. It was, it seems, a grief shared by a whole community, not a privilege of rank.
pageData.para3: The people themselves lived simply by the standards of later Andean civilization: no farming beyond a little cultivation, no pottery, no metal. They lived on the richest fishing ground in South America, the cold Humboldt Current, harvesting shellfish, sea lions and fish with bone hooks and nets, and hunting inland with spear-throwers. The Atacama Desert preserved what they left: tools, baskets, fishhooks, and the mummies themselves, buried in the dry sand above the shore.
pageData.para4: The Chinchorro tradition faded as new cultures, above all the ancestors of the great Andean states, spread through the valleys. But the mummies remained in the desert until modern archaeology brought them to light - some three hundred are known - and in 2021 the settlement and artificial mummification of the Chinchorro culture were inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List, honoring the oldest ritual of its kind known anywhere.
pageData.source1label: UNESCO: Settlement and Artificial Mummification of the Chinchorro Culture

pageData.title: The Marajoara Culture of Amazonia
pageData.titleline: The Marajoara Culture of Amazonia - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Marajoara Culture. At the mouth of the Amazon, where the river pours into the Atlantic, lies Marajo, an island the size of Switzerland, half drowned by the annual flood. Between about AD 400 and 1400, on this floodplain, the Marajoara built a civilization that overturned everything outsiders assumed about Amazonia: a populous, ranked society with chiefs, specialists and monumental earthworks, sustained not by clearing the forest but by mastering the flood.
pageData.para2: The Marajoara raised their world above the water. They built great artificial mounds - tesos - some rising twenty meters and covering hectares, on which stood their villages, ceremonial houses and the platforms of their leaders. Archaeologists count thousands of these earthworks across the island. The society was plainly stratified: the dead of the elite were buried in the great mounds in splendid painted urns, while commoners lay in simpler graves, and the size and number of the settlements imply tens of thousands of people under organized authority.
pageData.para3: Marajoara pottery is among the finest ever made in the ancient Americas: huge funerary urns painted in red, black and white, incised and modeled with serpents, human faces and female figures - the famous tangas and stools of the chiefs. Their subsistence was equally sophisticated: fish from the flood-pools, turtles, and crops including maize and, above all, management of the palms and flooded savannas - a productive system adapted to the várzea rather than destructive of it.
pageData.para4: Around 1400 the Marajoara culture waned, for reasons still debated, and the island passed to the Arua and other peoples whom the Portuguese met in the seventeenth century. The mounds were rediscovered by science in the nineteenth century, and the Marajoara have since become central to a revolution in Amazonian archaeology: the recognition that the greatest rainforest on earth once sustained complex, populous societies - not an untouched wilderness, but a worked and inhabited world.

pageData.title: San Agustin and the Upper Magdalena
pageData.titleline: San Agustin and the Upper Magdalena - The History Web
pageData.para1: San Agustin. In the high green valleys of the Upper Magdalena River, in what is now southern Colombia, a vanished people raised the greatest concentration of stone monuments in South America. Between about the first and the eighth centuries AD, the builders of San Agustin carved hundreds of colossal statues from volcanic rock - gods and guardians, warriors and mothers, jaguars, eagles and frogs - and set them over the tombs of their dead, beside temples and along the banks of the river whose source they revered.
pageData.para2: The statues are like nothing else in the Americas: slab-faced figures with staring eyes and bared fangs, some towering over seven meters, many carved with alter egos - a human figure crowned by a jaguar or bird-spirit - that scholars read as images of shamans and their transformations. The tombs they guarded were stone chambers under earthen mounds, and near them the San Agustin people shaped the landscape itself: ceremonial platforms, causeways, and the extraordinary carved stream-bed of Lavapatas, where figures and channels were cut into the living rock of the river.
pageData.para3: Of the builders themselves little is known directly. They were farmers of maize and beans, goldsmiths of skill, and traders on the routes between the Andes and the Amazon, and their society could command the labor to quarry, transport and raise stones weighing tons. They had no writing and left no name; even their language is lost. When their culture faded, around the eighth or ninth century, the forest covered the mounds, and local peoples who followed knew the statues only as the work of the ancients.
pageData.para4: The tombs were brought back to light from the eighteenth century onward - and plundered grievously before archaeologists could protect them. Today the San Agustin Archaeological Park and its sister sites preserve the largest group of religious monuments and megalithic sculptures in South America, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1995, and the emblem of Colombia's pre-Columbian past.
pageData.source2label: World History Encyclopedia: The Megalithic Funerary Art of San Agustin

pageData.title: El Paraiso and the First Coastal Temples
pageData.titleline: El Paraiso and the First Coastal Temples - The History Web
pageData.para1: El Paraiso. A few miles from the mouth of the Chillon River, just north of modern Lima, stands the largest monument of the age before pottery on the coast of Peru: El Paraiso, a complex of massive stone-and-adobe platforms raised around 1800 BC. It belongs to the same astonishing world as Caral, the Preceramic period, when the people of the Peruvian coast - living on fish from the cold current and cotton from the river valleys - built some of the earliest monumental architecture in the Americas centuries before they fired a pot.
pageData.para2: The site covers more than fifty hectares, with a dozen mounds arranged around a central plaza, the largest structures standing over ten meters high. Its builders worked without metal, wheels or beasts of burden: the platforms were raised from hundreds of thousands of tons of quarried stone and adobe, carried in woven shicra bags and laid with clay mortar, then plastered and painted in vivid reds and yellows. Within the main temple, archaeologists uncovered the remains of painted friezes - and, in later levels, the haunting image of a figure with upraised arms.
pageData.para3: What El Paraiso was for is still argued. It had few signs of permanent residence: no dense middens, no houses on the scale of the platforms. Most scholars read it as a ceremonial and pilgrimage center, a meeting place where the fishing villages and farming hamlets of the lower Chillon gathered for rites and feasts - a pattern, temple first and city later, that would recur along the Peruvian coast for three thousand years.
pageData.para4: El Paraiso was abandoned around the time pottery transformed Andean life, and the desert preserved it almost intact for four thousand years. It now lies within the growing outskirts of Lima, threatened and protected in turn, and stands with Caral as testimony that civilization in the Americas began not with farms and pots, but with fish, cotton - and the impulse to build together.

pageData.title: The Lima Culture
pageData.titleline: The Lima Culture - The History Web
pageData.para1: The Lima Culture. Between about AD 200 and 700, while the Moche ruled the northern coast of Peru, the central coast - the valleys of the Chillon, Rimac and Lurin, the ground on which the city of Lima now stands - was home to its own civilization: the Lima culture. It was a society of farmers and priests fed by irrigation canals drawn from the rivers, organized around great stepped pyramids of adobe brick, each raised in stages over the centuries, each the temple of its valley.
pageData.para2: The greatest of these monuments survive inside the modern city: Huaca Pucllana, the vast stepped platform of adobe that towers over the Miraflores district, was the ceremonial heart of a Lima-culture town, a place of offerings and ritual banquets where the priesthood received the labor and tribute of the valleys. At its altars the Lima people sacrificed fine pottery, woven textiles, and - as the excavated tombs show - human victims and great jars of sharks and other offerings to the sea that fed them.
pageData.para3: Lima-culture art has a style all its own: pottery painted with the interlocking, serpentine figures scholars call the interlocking style, and above all the cult of the sea-bird and marine life that runs through its iconography. Its people wove superb textiles, fished the Humboldt Current, and buried their dead in the platforms with offerings of food, cloth and ceramics. They traded and contended with their neighbors - the Nazca to the south, the rising highland powers of Wari.
pageData.para4: By about AD 700 the Lima culture was absorbed into the expanding Wari sphere, and its valley temples passed to later peoples. The adobe pyramids remained - some fifty huacas still stand within metropolitan Lima, and Huaca Pucllana, excavated since the 1980s, is now the most visited pre-Columbian monument of the Peruvian capital: a temple of the civilization on whose ground, quite literally, the city was built.
